supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a real angular frequency $\omega\in\mathbb R$ and a bounded open region $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ with $C^1$ boundary in a material-rest frame. Here a material-rest frame is the inertial frame in which every modelled material element has fixed spatial coordinates, as stipulated by the framework's material-closure postulate. A map in $C^1(\overline\Omega)$ means the restriction of a $C^1$ map on an open neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$. Let $\varepsilon,\mu:\overline\Omega\to\mathbb C^{3\times3}$ be continuous coefficient fields with units $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$. They may be spatially varying and complex. Let $E_j,H_j\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$ and $J_j\in C^0(\overline\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$, for $j=1,2$, be phasor amplitudes with SI units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$. The corresponding real fields use $e^{-i\omega t}$, for example $E_j^{\mathrm{real}}(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(E_j(x)e^{-i\omega t})$. Their displacement and magnetic-induction amplitudes are $D_j=\varepsilon E_j$ in $\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}$ and $B_j=\mu H_j$ in $\mathrm T$.

The fixed-frequency constitutive and source equations are

$$D_j=\varepsilon E_j,\qquad B_j=\mu H_j,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E_j=i\omega B_j,\qquad \operatorname{curl}H_j=J_j-i\omega D_j.$$

All operators act componentwise on the spatial variable. For $u,v\in\mathbb C^3$, define the **bilinear** dot product $u\cdot v=\sum_{r=1}^3u_rv_r$ and the complex-bilinear cross product by the usual right-handed component formula. Neither product conjugates either input. The transpose $T$ is the ordinary matrix transpose, without complex conjugation. This definition calls the coefficient model **reciprocal** when $\varepsilon(x)^T=\varepsilon(x)$ and $\mu(x)^T=\mu(x)$ at every $x\in\overline\Omega$. It places no Hermitian, positive-definite, or passivity condition on these complex matrices.

This is a fixed-frequency phasor data class. Its possibly complex coefficients are not inferred from the framework's real, instantaneous material branch; a separate response model is required to justify any such interpretation.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded domain with $C^1$ boundary and outward unit normal $n$. Fix a real angular frequency $\omega$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Let $E_j,H_j\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$ and $J_j\in C^0(\overline\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$, for $j=1,2$, be phasor fields and electric-current densities in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, respectively. Suppose both pairs solve the fixed-frequency Maxwell equations there with the same continuous coefficient maps $\varepsilon,\mu:\overline\Omega\to\mathbb C^{3\times3}$ and $\varepsilon(x)^T=\varepsilon(x)$, $\mu(x)^T=\mu(x)$ at every $x$. Use Euclidean volume measure $dV$ and boundary area measure $dS$. Then

$$\int_{\partial\Omega}n\cdot(E_1\times H_2-E_2\times H_1)\,dS=\int_\Omega(E_2\cdot J_1-E_1\cdot J_2)\,dV.$$

The dot and cross products in this identity are the complex-bilinear products defined in the reciprocal phasor model; no complex conjugation occurs. Both integrals have units W. In particular, the real symmetric positive permittivity tensor and positive scalar permeability of the lossless anisotropic plane-wave model satisfy these reciprocal-coefficient hypotheses, so the identity applies to any two such phasor solutions restricted to a bounded $C^1$ subdomain.

Use the finite-energy boundary model defined earlier on the nonempty open time interval $I$ and bounded Lipschitz polyhedron $\Omega$. Thus $\varepsilon,\mu$ are time-independent real symmetric essentially bounded coefficient fields with uniform positive lower bounds, $E,H\in C^1(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))\cap C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega))$, $J\in C(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$, and

$$\varepsilon\partial_tE=\operatorname{curl}H-J,\qquad\mu\partial_tH=-\operatorname{curl}E$$

hold as $L^2$ identities for every $t\in I$. Define

$$W(t):=\frac12\int_\Omega\bigl(E\cdot\varepsilon E+H\cdot\mu H\bigr)\,d\lambda_3.$$

For every $s<t$ in $I$, the closure-defined PEC branch satisfies

$$W(t)-W(s)=-\int_s^t\int_\Omega E\cdot J\,d\lambda_3\,dr.$$

For the Green-compatible impedance branch, where $H_\tau=Y(n\times E_\tau)$, it satisfies

$$W(t)-W(s)=-\int_s^t\int_\Omega E\cdot J\,d\lambda_3\,dr-\int_s^t\int_{\partial\Omega}Y|E_\tau|^2\,dS\,dr.$$

Here $E_\tau,H_\tau$ and the Green identity are exactly the $L^2$ boundary data and admissibility condition in the model definition; no trace is inferred from H(curl) membership alone. The work density $E\cdot J$ has SI units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$; the boundary term has units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ per unit area and is nonnegative in the impedance branch. If $J=0$ and $E(t_0)=H(t_0)=0$ in $L^2$, the only admissible solution is zero for $t\ge t_0$. Uniqueness is forward from the specified initial time; no backward uniqueness is asserted for a dissipative boundary.

Work in a material rest frame: an inertial frame in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$ and history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$, as defined by the framework's earlier material-closure formulation. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be the material region in that frame and $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open time interval. The electric field $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, polarization fields $P_\ell:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, and magnetic fields $B,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial-vector fields in that frame. At every fixed $x\in\Omega$, require $E(x,\cdot)\in C^0(I;\mathbb R^3)$ and $P_\ell(x,\cdot)\in C^2(I;\mathbb R^3)$ for each $1\le\ell\le N$, so the displayed time derivatives are classical. These are time-regularity conditions only; this postulate imposes no spatial regularity, which must be stated separately wherever a consuming field-equation result requires it. In SI, $E$ is in V m$^{-1}$, $P_\ell$ in C m$^{-2}$, $B$ in T and $H$ in A m$^{-1}$.

For a fixed finite integer $N\ge1$, adopt at every material point $x$ the constitutive equations

$$D(x,t)=\varepsilon_\infty E(x,t)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}P_\ell(x,t),\qquad B(x,t)=\mu H(x,t),$$

$$\partial_t^2P_\ell(x,t)+\gamma_\ell\partial_tP_\ell(x,t)+\omega_\ell^2P_\ell(x,t)=a_\ell E(x,t)\qquad (1\le\ell\le N).$$

Here $\varepsilon_\infty>0$ is a constant scalar with units F m$^{-1}$, $\mu>0$ is a constant scalar with units H m$^{-1}$, $a_\ell>0$ are constant parameters with units F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $\omega_\ell>0$ are constant angular frequencies with units s$^{-1}$, and $\gamma_\ell\ge0$ are constant damping rates with units s$^{-1}$. The parameters are independent of position and time; this is the meaning of homogeneous in this model. The model is linear because all displayed field and oscillator relations are linear with fixed coefficients, and spatially local because the oscillator equation at $x$ uses only the field and oscillator state at that same $x$. The magnetic law has only the constant scalar coefficient $\mu$ and no independent magnetic polarization variable; this is the nonmagnetic oscillator model adopted here.

The word nonmagnetic here means that the oscillator sector has no dynamic magnetic response; the fixed scalar coefficient $\mu$ can still encode a separate static constitutive response. To identify the displayed quantities with the framework's macroscopic definitions, stipulate $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\varepsilon_\infty-\varepsilon_0)E+\sum_{\ell=1}^N P_\ell$ and $M_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\mu_0^{-1}-\mu^{-1})B$. Then $D=\varepsilon_0E+P_{\mathrm{tot}}=\varepsilon_\infty E+\sum P_\ell$ and $H=\mu_0^{-1}B-M_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mu^{-1}B$. This is a constitutive identification in the model, not a microscopic decomposition.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, the oscillator state consists of $P_\ell(x,t_0)$ and $\partial_tP_\ell(x,t_0)$. For a selected causal zero-past branch, choose an onset $\tau\in I$ and require $E(x,t)=0$ and $P_\ell(x,t)=\partial_tP_\ell(x,t)=0$ for every $t\in I$ with $t\le\tau$. Continuity gives $E(x,\tau)=0$, and the equation gives $\partial_t^2P_\ell(x,\tau)=0$, consistent with the $C^2$ zero extension through onset. For $t\ge\tau$ this branch is the retarded initial-value equation with those data, so its value at time $t$ uses the applied field only on $[\tau,t]$. If $\gamma_\ell=0$, no decaying stationary impulse response is assumed; in particular, this is not an absolutely integrable convolution for arbitrary bounded histories. This postulate does not assert that any actual material realizes the equations.

Use a material rest frame: an inertial frame in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$ and history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$, as defined by the framework's earlier material-closure formulation. In that frame, let $E,P:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be the electric field and polarization, and let $V:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a free-carrier current density. At every fixed $x\in\Omega$, require $E(x,\cdot)\in C^0(I;\mathbb R^3)$ and $P(x,\cdot),V(x,\cdot)\in C^1(I;\mathbb R^3)$, so the displayed time derivatives are classical. From [L1] and [A1] or [A2], respectively, the field and constitutive equations give $\varepsilon_\infty\partial_tE=\operatorname{curl}H-J_{\mathrm{tot}}$ and $\mu\partial_tH=-\operatorname{curl}E$.

In the Lorentz branch, dot the $\ell$th oscillator equation [A1] with $\partial_tP_\ell/a_\ell$. Since $a_\ell>0$, the division is valid; the product rule in [F2] gives $E\cdot\partial_tP_\ell=\partial_t\!\left((|\partial_tP_\ell|^2+\omega_\ell^2|P_\ell|^2)/(2a_\ell)\right)+(\gamma_\ell/a_\ell)|\partial_tP_\ell|^2$. The last term is nonnegative because $\gamma_\ell\ge0$.

In the Drude branch, dot $\partial_tV+\gamma V=aE$ from [A2] with $V/a$. The product rule and $a>0$ give $E\cdot V=\partial_t(|V|^2/(2a))+(\gamma/a)|V|^2$, whose last term is nonnegative because $\gamma\ge0$.

Define the field energy density $u_f:\overline\Omega\times\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ by $u_f=(\varepsilon_\infty|E|^2+\mu|H|^2)/2$. Differentiate it componentwise using [F2] and the field equations of step 1.1. This gives $\partial_tu_f=E\cdot\operatorname{curl}H-E\cdot J_{\mathrm{tot}}-H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E$. Applying [F1] yields $-\operatorname{div}(E\times H)-E\cdot J_f-\sum E\cdot\partial_tP_\ell$ in the Lorentz branch and $-\operatorname{div}(E\times H)-E\cdot J_f-E\cdot V$ in the Drude branch.

Define the total field-plus-material energy density $u:\overline\Omega\times\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ branchwise: in the Lorentz branch, $u:=u_f+\sum_{\ell=1}^M\bigl(|\partial_tP_\ell|^2+\omega_\ell^2|P_\ell|^2\bigr)/(2a_\ell)$; in the Drude branch, $u:=u_f+|V|^2/(2a)$. All terms are nonnegative, have SI units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and are jointly smooth and $T$-periodic under the Statement's hypotheses. Substituting step 1.2 into the Lorentz field balance of step 2.1 cancels every $E\cdot\partial_tP_\ell$ term; substituting step 1.3 into its Drude balance cancels $E\cdot V$. Since the given source-free condition has $J_f=0$, each branch therefore satisfies $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}(E\times H)=-\ell$ with exactly the loss density $\ell$ in the Statement.

Integrate the local identity of step 3.1 over $\Omega$ at each time and apply [F3] to $E\times H$. Then integrate in time from $0$ to $T$. statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix a real angular frequency $\omega>0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and use the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention and SI field units of the fixed-frequency reciprocal-phasor model. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded device region with $C^1$ boundary in one stationary material-rest frame. Its continuous phasor coefficient maps are $\varepsilon,\mu:\overline\Omega\to\mathbb C^{3\times3}$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, respectively. The complex phasor fields $\widetilde E,\widetilde H\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$ have units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$. They satisfy the fixed-frequency Maxwell equations of the reciprocal-phasor data class, with no impressed volume current or charge in $\Omega$. The corresponding real fields are $E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ and $H(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde H(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, with period $T=2\pi/\omega$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined by the countable-choice axiom when the reciprocal boundary identity below is used.

An **admissible port** consists of a bounded connected $C^1$ cross-section $\Sigma_j$ in a plane perpendicular to a fixed unit guide axis $\widehat z_j$, together with a uniform lossless straight reference guide extending from that section. The outward normal $n_j$ on the port points from $\Omega$ into the guide. The reference-guide phasor coefficients and wall conditions are independent of distance along $\widehat z_j$. A propagating channel mode is a pair of $C^1$ complex transverse profiles $(e_{j\alpha},h_{j\alpha})$ whose associated source-free phasor fields in the guide solve the fixed-frequency Maxwell equations and have longitudinal factor $e^{\pm i\beta_\alpha s_j}$ with real $\beta_\alpha>0$ in $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. The profiles are normalized per unit amplitude in $\mathrm{W^{1/2}}$, so the resulting fields have units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$. The plus and minus signs are assigned according to whether energy travels toward or away from $\Omega$. At $\omega$, assume a finite list of $N$ propagating mode channels in total and that this list is complete for the propagating channels represented by the finite interface. Any outgoing radiation continuum or omitted propagating channel is separately recorded as nonnegative outward power $P_{\mathrm{other}}$. Evanescent modes may be required in the exact near-port matching field, but are not entries of the propagating amplitude vectors; no finite truncation of such matching modes is asserted to be exact.

Let $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_N)^T\in\mathbb C^N$ and $b=(b_1,\ldots,b_N)^T\in\mathbb C^N$ be the incoming and outgoing amplitudes. Choose the mode shapes and amplitude convention so that each coefficient has units $\mathrm{W^{1/2}}$, the Hermitian norm is $\|a\|_2^2=\sum_{\alpha=1}^N|a_\alpha|^2$ in W, and the total time-averaged outward power through the port sections is

$$P_{\mathrm{ports}}=\|b\|_2^2-\|a\|_2^2.$$

This equality, including the vanishing of cross terms in the real-power pairing, is a port-mode normalization hypothesis. For complex phasor fields the time-averaged Poynting vector is $\boldsymbol\Pi=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde E\times\widetilde H^*)$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, where $*$ denotes componentwise conjugation before the bilinear cross product. This Hermitian power pairing is distinct from the unconjugated Lorentz bilinear pairing.

On the non-port wall $\Gamma_w$, the model prescribes either a smooth PEC condition $E_\tau(t)=0$, giving zero outward wall power, or a passive wall condition with explicitly specified nonnegative cycle-averaged outward power $P_\partial\ge0$. Here $E_\tau(t)=E(t)-(n\cdot E(t))n$ and $H_\tau(t)=H(t)-(n\cdot H(t))n$ are the classical tangential restrictions of the smooth real fields. A smooth impedance wall is one such condition: for a real scalar surface admittance $Y\ge0$ in siemens and $H_\tau(t)=Y(n\times E_\tau(t))$, its instantaneous outward power density is $n\cdot(E_\tau(t)\times H_\tau(t))=Y|E_\tau(t)|^2\ge0$, so its cycle-averaged outward power is nonnegative. For phasor amplitude $\widetilde E_\tau$, that average is $\tfrac12Y|\widetilde E_\tau|^2$. This is a smooth-field model assumption; no $L^2$ trace is inferred from membership in $H(\operatorname{curl})$.

The total cycle-averaged outward boundary power is the port contribution $\|b\|_2^2-\|a\|_2^2$, plus $P_\partial$ and any unlisted outgoing power $P_{\mathrm{other}}$. No unlisted incoming power is included.

For each $a$, assume the adopted linear source-free Maxwell boundary problem has a unique time-harmonic solution and a unique outgoing vector $b$. The model assumes no incoming wave in unlisted channels. By linearity of the phasor equations and uniqueness, the map $a\mapsto b$ is complex-linear: a linear combination of two solutions solves the problem for the same linear combination of their incoming data, and uniqueness identifies its outgoing data.
